<reason>PRO won a tight, high-quality exchange by neutralizing CON's two structural objections and leaving one strong CON argument only partially standing. CON's "the disclosure is already on the shelf" line was damaged by PRO's level-vs-change distinction; CON's "sideways comparison" reply was clever but incomplete, since shoppers also decide whether a product remains worth buying at all, and PRO's was/now example showed the industry itself knows delta framing is what gets read and deploys it selectively. CON's compliance-manual attack was the sharpest pressure of the debate, but PRO's A1 answer (baseline is the weight-change event, promotions change price not weight) was clean and directly responsive. CON's best live route—substitution toward ingredient downgrades—was never fully refuted causally, but CON weakened it with an inconsistent "status quo catches the shrink" answer (contradicting its own inattention premise) and a "no gain" claim on the headline-price route that ignores the transparency gain of moving cost recovery from a hidden to a visible channel. Both sides used proper Q/A format and both had Rebuttal 2 clipped. PRO's "manufactured inattention" frame made the decision cleaner than CON's "follow the cost" close.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A4.1/A4.4 answer to CON's baseline pressure: defining the trigger as the weight-change event rather than a date defused the "which baseline?" attack, and the "was £2.00, now £1.50" example turned CON's inattention argument into evidence of selective salience—CON's "museum, not a shelf" reply was witty but didn't rebut that the industry uses delta framing whenever it helps them.</best_rebuttal>
